units.summary: Avimi forgets his learning and travels to his student Rav Hisda to recall it, later demonstrating the laws of the meal offering to Rav Nahman using a physical vessel.
Rabbi Yoḥanan silences Reish Lakish with an objection, an event later analyzed and contested by Rav Pappa and Rav Yosef bar Shemaya.
Rav Dimi arrives from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia and reports Rabbi Elazar's legal view on the meal offering of a sinner.

A man planted seeds in his neighbor's vineyard while the grapes were budding, leading the Sages to rule on the prohibition of the seeds versus the vines. An incident where a man planted seeds in a friend's vineyard while the grapes were budding was brought before the Sages, who ruled the seeds forbidden but the vines permitted.
The Gemara repeats the incident of the man who planted seeds in his friend's vineyard to challenge a legal inference.

Yosef the Babylonian repeatedly questions Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua on a ruling until the sage realizes his error, leading to an emotional moment where the sage weeps and praises the students' love for Torah.
Ben Bukhri testifies in Yavne that priests are not required to pay the half-shekel, and Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai disputes his interpretation of the law.
Rav Kahana travels from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael and encounters the sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya engaged in a legal discussion about meal offerings.
The Gemara recounts how the Hasmonean kings, lacking gold, fashioned the Temple Candelabrum out of iron spits and plated them with tin.
An incident is recounted where the Temple Candelabrum was found to be slightly too heavy and was refined in a furnace until it reached the exact weight of Moses' Candelabrum.
Rabbi Yosei relates that God sent fiery models of the Ark, Table, and Candelabrum from heaven so Moses could see and replicate them.
The angel Gabriel dressed as a craftsman to demonstrate the construction of the Candelabrum to Moses.
Moses struggled to understand the form of the Candelabrum, the moon, and creeping animals until God pointed them out to him.

Agra discovers a hole in a letter in his phylacteries and brings the case to Rabbi Abba for a ruling. Agra brings his damaged phylacteries to Rabbi Abba, who provides a ruling on whether the damaged letter heh is still valid.
Rami bar Tamrei brings damaged phylacteries to Rabbi Zeira, who instructs him to have a child read the letter to determine its status.
Moses ascends to heaven, is shown the future greatness and tragic death of Rabbi Akiva, and is told to accept the divine will without question.
Agra brings a Torah scroll with extra letters to Rabbi Abba, who rules that such errors can be corrected, unlike missing letters.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri recounts a time his untithed produce was mixed with tithed produce and he sought a practical solution from Rabbi Tarfon.
Rabbi Helbo reports witnessing Rav Huna's specific method of rolling a mezuza, which is then contrasted with a baraita describing Rabbi Meir's habitual practice of writing mezuzot.
Rav Helbo recounts seeing Rav Huna overturn a jug to hold a Torah scroll so that he could sit on his bed without sitting on the same level as the scroll.
The Gemara mentions an incident where Rabbi Elazar recoiled upon realizing he was sitting on a bed that had a Torah scroll on it.
The Exilarch asks Rav Nahman to affix mezuzot to his new house, but Rav Nahman tells him to hang the doors first so the placement can be determined correctly.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef reports that the mezuzot in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house were placed horizontally.
Abaye reports seeing that the porticos in Rabbah's house did not have mezuzot even though they had doorposts.
Rav Pappa visits Mar Shmuel's home, observes a mezuza affixed to an entrance with only one doorpost, and questions the legal basis for this practice.
A student of Rabbi Akiva tied his phylacteries with blue wool, and Rabbi Akiva observed him but did not object, serving as a precedent for the law.
Hyrcanus, the son of Rabbi Eliezer, tied his phylacteries with purple wool, and his father did not correct him.
While Abaye is studying with Rav Yosef, his phylactery strap tears, leading to a ruling that he may not simply tie it back together.

Passage B features a different set of actors (Rav Aha and Rav Ashi) and a different proposed solution (sewing vs. tying) to the same legal problem, following the common Talmudic pattern of grouping similar incidents.
Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna are observed praying the evening service while wearing their phylacteries.
Ravina observes Rav Ashi donning phylacteries after dark and questions him, leading Rav Ashi to explain he is doing so to safeguard them.
Peleimu asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about a two-headed man and is rebuked for asking a ridiculous question, only for a man to arrive immediately reporting the birth of such a child.
Rav Ashi observes that Ameimar's phylacteries are visible through a tear in his sleeve while sitting before him.
Ravina observes Mar bar Rav Ashi's ritual fringes tear in public on Shabbat but waits until they reach his home to inform him to avoid public embarrassment.
Ravina observes Mar bar Rav Ashi's ritual fringes tear in public on Shabbat and questions why he did not remove the garment immediately, leading to a discussion on human dignity.
Levi tells Shmuel not to sit down until he explains the reasoning behind a specific Mishnaic ruling regarding ritual fringes.
While Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana are sitting together, a man passes by wearing a unique sky-blue cloak with ritual fringes, prompting their evaluation.
Rabbi Zeira untied and removed the ritual fringes from his linen cloak in response to a rabbinic decree.
The early pious men would affix ritual fringes to their garments as soon as they had woven a small portion of the cloth.
Rabba bar Huna visits Rava bar Rav Naḥman, notices his ritual fringes are invalid due to how the cloak is folded, and Rava bar Rav Naḥman responds by discarding the garment.
An angel confronts Rav Ketina for wearing garments that exempt him from the requirement of ritual fringes, warning him of divine wrath.
The Gemara records the different physical methods Rav Yehuda, Rav Hanina, and Ravina used to protect their ritual fringes when sending garments to be laundered.

While sitting before Rav Ashi, Rav Samma challenges Ravina for having ritual fringes too close to the edge of his torn cloak, but becomes embarrassed when he realizes his error, prompting Rav Ashi to comfort him.
Rav Nahman encounters Rav Adda bar Ahava reciting a blessing while affixing fringes and informs him that Rav ruled no blessing is required.
Following the death of Rav Huna, Rav Hisda enters the study hall to raise a contradiction between two rulings of Rav regarding blessings on ritual fringes.
Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rav Yehuda, describes or performs a chemical test to verify the authenticity of tekhelet dye using a specific solution and overnight soaking.
Mar of Mashkhei brought wool to Rav Ahai's academy that failed one dye test but passed another, leading Rav Ahai to rule the wool fit and clarify the relationship between the tests.
Rabbi Mani was careful to buy wool according to the stringencies of the baraita, and an old man told him that his ancestors did the same and succeeded.
Rav Yehuda would put ritual fringes on his wife's cloak and recite a blessing every morning, a practice the Gemara analyzes to determine his legal stance on women's obligations.
When King David felt distressed while standing naked in a bathhouse without visible mitzvot, he remembered his circumcision and was comforted.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Rav Avya would specifically eat spices and fruit on Shabbat to ensure he reached the daily quota of one hundred blessings.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya’akov questions his son's choice of blessing, leading to a discussion on which blessings are appropriate.
A man's ritual fringes physically prevent him from sinning with a famous prostitute, leading her to renounce her wealth, convert to Judaism, and marry him.

Rav Yehuda recounts how Ḥanina ben Ḥizkiyya prevented the suppression of the Book of Ezekiel by isolating himself in an upper chamber with three hundred jars of oil to resolve its contradictions with the Torah.
Ben Bukhri testifies in Yavne regarding priestly contributions to the half-shekel, and Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai corrects his assertion.
A Tanna recites a ruling about disqualified offerings before Rav Nahman, who questions the logic and identifies the teaching as belonging to the school of Rabba bar Avuh.
Rabbi Abbahu explains the history of the High Priest's meal offering funding, which shifted from public to private and back to public due to treasury shortages and subsequent heir negligence.
When the Sages present Rava's legal proof to Rabbi Yirmeya, Yirmeya insults the Babylonians' intelligence, leading Rava to defend his reputation and the quality of his legal traditions.

Rabbi Perida initially questions the worthiness of Rabbi Ezra who is waiting at his door, but upon admitting him and seeing his embarrassment, Perida comforts him with a homily, leading to a mutual exchange of teachings.
When the Temple is destroyed, Abraham confronts God to advocate for his children, eventually mourning their fate until a Divine Voice promises their eventual restoration.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya’akov would wave his lulav and declare that he was shooting an arrow into the eye of Satan, a practice the Gemara subsequently discourages.

During a Hasmonean civil war, an elderly man uses Greek wisdom to advise the besiegers to stop providing sacrificial animals, leading to a pig being sent up and a subsequent rabbinic curse on Greek wisdom.
When the Sages cannot find barley for the omer, a mute man uses gestures to lead Mordekhai to the location of Gaggot Tzerifin.
In a parallel to the previous story, Mordekhai interprets the gestures of a deaf-mute man to find grain for the two loaves in Ein Sokher.
Mordekhai correctly interprets the ambiguous language of three women bringing bird offerings, proving they were thanks-offerings for surviving danger rather than sin-offerings.

Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai confronts the Boethusians over their calendar laws, silencing the group until one elderly man steps forward to argue with him. Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai concludes a confrontation with a Boethusian elder who challenged his rhetorical defense of the Pharisaic calendar.
Rava expresses a pious wish to receive a legal answer in a dream before continuing his halakhic analysis.
Different groups of rabbis ate the new crop at different times based on their legal interpretations of its prohibition status.
Ravina's mother reports to him that his father followed a specific stringent practice regarding the timing of eating the new crop.
Yehuda bar Neḥemya silences Rabbi Tarfon in a legal debate, causing his face to brighten with pride, which leads Rabbi Akiva to rebuke him and predict his short life.
A baraita recounts an incident where wolves swallowed two children and excreted them across the Jordan, leading the Sages to rule on the ritual purity of the remains.
The Gemara cites an incident where wheat rained from the sky onto Adi the Arab, covering a large area.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls how he and his fellow students would carry oil and towels across various domains to serve Rabbi Shimon while studying in Tekoa.
When Rabbi Abba suggests that a certain offering is scattered to be wasted, the Sages laugh at him and question the existence of such a practice in the Temple.
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate the consecration of loaves for a blemished offering until Rabbi Eliezer is silenced by a counter-argument and concedes.
Rabba retracts his legal opinion to align with Rava based on Rabbi Eliezer's earlier concession.
Abaye and the Sages visit the ailing Rav Ila and engage in a legal discussion regarding remedies for a thanks offering.
Ravina visits Dimhorya and Rav Dimi proposes a legal solution which Ravina rejects based on a verse.
Rabbi Elazar explains that he saw Rabbi Yoḥanan in a dream and was thereby inspired to provide the reasoning for Rabbi Yoḥanan's legal position.
The Egyptian sorcerers Yohana and Mamre mock Moses for bringing 'straw to Aforayim' (magic to the land of magic), and Moses retorts that one brings merchandise to where it is in demand.
Rav Ḥilkiya bar Tovi followed a specific biennial plowing and sowing cycle which resulted in a doubled yield of high-quality wheat that he sold for fine flour.

A messenger seeking a vast quantity of oil travels through several cities before finding a humble-looking farmer in Gush Chalav who provides an immense supply and even extends credit, proving the agricultural richness of Asher's territory.
Rav Yosef would hoe his orchard land extra thoroughly, which resulted in the production of exceptionally strong wine.
Rav Pappa relates that Rava tested the students with a legal question regarding the libations of a ewe.
Reish Lakish becomes angry when Rabbi Elazar repeats his teaching without attribution, leading to a confrontation where Reish Lakish overwhelms him with objections before eventually reconciling.
Ben Dama asks his uncle Rabbi Yishmael if he may study Greek wisdom since he has already mastered the Torah, and Rabbi Yishmael rebukes him using a verse.
The Gemara records an incident where priests mistakenly identified moonlight as dawn, leading them to prematurely slaughter the daily offering, which then had to be destroyed.

After reporting a case where the Sages measured the blood of a dead mule from the Nasi's house, Rabbi Beivai is challenged by a contradictory tradition and falls silent, explaining that his poverty prevents him from concentrating on the debate.

A story continuing from the previous page about a dead mule in the Nasi's house leads to a legal challenge that Rabbi Beivai is too impoverished and distracted to answer, eventually resolved by Rav Yosef.
The Gemara recounts the death of Shimon HaTzaddik and the subsequent treacherous rivalry between his sons Onias and Shimi, which led to the establishment of the Temple of Onias in Egypt.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perahya remarks on how his attitude toward holding high office changed once he attained it.
Onias and his followers travel to Alexandria and establish an altar for sacrifices.
